data.hypothesis: Grouping four neighboring j outputs in each CTA may amortize repeated gy loads while retaining a direct FP32 reduction over B and L for each output. The extra accumulators and four shared-memory reductions per CTA could offset that reuse. Earlier valid results show the one-stage CTA parent at 0.014375 s and the split-scratch variant at 0.019781 s mean complete-call time; this contrasting experiment avoids another scratch stage and must be judged on complete-call timing and correctness.

memory_lessons.applicability: For this campaign's complete-call protocol, the measured split-scratch candidate was slower than the one-stage CTA candidate; that does not isolate the weight-gradient kernel or prove split reductions are generally slower.
memory_lessons.claim: The valid one-stage CTA candidate measured 0.014375 s mean, while the valid 65,536-element tiled partial-sum candidate measured 0.019781 s mean.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Compare a direct CTA that computes four neighboring j outputs and reuses each gy value against the one-stage parent using the same correctness checks and complete-call timing.

data.notes: This changes only the weight-gradient kernel: each CTA handles four adjacent j values, reads gy once per sample for that group, and independently reduces four FP32 accumulators. Every valid gk entry is written during the call; scratch is neither read nor written. The catalog contains two distinct valid programs, but their timings are complete-call measurements and do not attribute cost to this kernel. No performance outcome is claimed for this candidate.
transformations: Changed the weight-gradient kernel to assign each CTA four neighboring j outputs for one h.
Each CTA traverses B and L using the existing thread layout, reuses one gy load across the four output accumulators, and performs four independent shared-memory FP32 reductions.
Preserved bounds checks and writes every valid gk output; the variant does not use scratch or allocate additional memory.
